Essays & Series

Writing

Longer explanatory writing on statistics and machine learning, for ideas that need more room than a paper or a talk allows.

Interactive series · 9 parts · November 2026

Notes on the Deep Learning Tuning Playbook

Google Research's Deep Learning Tuning Playbook (Godbole, Dahl, Gilmer, Shallue and Nado, 2023) collects years of practical experience training neural networks into short, concrete rules, such as re-tuning the learning rate whenever the batch size changes and scoring a run by its best checkpoint rather than its last. Each rule fits in a sentence, but the reasons behind it usually do not.

In this series I work through those reasons. Each part takes a group of the Playbook's recommendations, writes down a simple model of the mechanism behind them, and uses small interactive simulations to show when and why the advice holds.

Start with Part 1Introduction & overview

Rules, glossary & references · The original Playbook on GitHub ↗

Contents

Act I

Experimental method and setup

How to run experiments you can trust, and the decisions made once at the start of a project.

  1. 01Tuning a network one question at a timeThe incremental tuning loop, scoring a run by its best checkpoint, and the roles that make comparisons fair.
  2. 02Starting a new projectWhy to begin with a proven architecture, a popular optimizer and a deliberately simple first configuration.
  3. 03Choosing the batch sizeThe batch size sets training speed and cost, and the hardware and gradient noise set which sizes are worth using.
Act II

Running, reading and deciding

How to place the trials in a round of experiments, check what comes back, and decide what to keep.

  1. 04Where to put your trials, and how many to runGrid, random and quasi-random search, when Bayesian optimization fits, and how many trials a study needs.
  2. 05Reading the results of a tuning studyChecking search-space boundaries and training curves before trusting the best trial, then comparing with isolation plots.
  3. 06Deciding whether to adopt a changeSeed-to-seed variation, re-running the best trial, and weighing a gain against the complexity it adds.
Act III

Dynamics, stability and engineering

How long to train, how to keep training stable, and the pipeline every round depends on.

  1. 07How long to trainSetting the number of training steps, with and without a compute limit, and adjusting the learning-rate schedule to match.
  2. 08Finding and fixing training instabilitiesRecognizing an unstable run, and how learning-rate warmup and gradient clipping let a larger learning rate train.
  3. 09Input pipelines, evaluation, checkpoints and multi-host trainingInput bottlenecks, periodic evaluation, checkpoints, experiment tracking, batch normalization and multi-host setups.
